layers.name: Average temperature
layers.definition: Average yearly air temperature across the country
layers.explanation: Burkina Faso, Mali, Senegal and Mauritania in the Sahel average around 29 degrees Celsius over the year. Greenland averages below -18, and Canada and Russia are below zero because so much of their land is Arctic. Latitude, altitude and the oceans explain the map.

layers.name: Carbon dioxide from cement
layers.definition: Carbon dioxide released by making cement, per person a year

source.name: Our World in Data (Global Carbon Project)

layers.explanation: Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Cyprus, Laos, the United Arab Emirates and Oman release the most cement carbon per person, through building booms and export plants. Many small islands and Afghanistan make no cement at all. China and Vietnam are high among large countries, while most of Africa is low.

layers.name: Carbon dioxide per person
layers.definition: Carbon dioxide emitted from fossil fuels and industry per person a year

source.name: Our World in Data (Global Carbon Project)

layers.explanation: Qatar, Brunei, Kuwait, Trinidad and Tobago and Bahrain emit more than 24 tonnes per person a year, driven by oil, gas and petrochemicals. The Democratic Republic of the Congo, Burundi, Somalia and the Central African Republic emit under 0.1. The Gulf, North America and Australia sit at the top, with most of sub-Saharan Africa at the bottom.

layers.name: Coal electricity
layers.definition: Share of electricity from coal

source.name: Our World in Data (Energy Institute, Ember)

layers.explanation: Botswana, Mongolia, South Africa and India burn coal for more than 70% of their electricity, and Poland, China and Kazakhstan are also high. Countries with big rivers, gas fields or no coal of their own have none. The pattern follows where coal is dug up more than how rich a country is.

layers.name: Carbon dioxide since 1750
layers.definition: All carbon dioxide emitted from fossil fuels and industry since 1750
layers.unit: Millions of tonnes, added up over all years.

source.name: Our World in Data (Global Carbon Project)

layers.explanation: The United States has emitted about 425 billion tonnes since 1750, China about 260 billion, and Russia, Germany, the United Kingdom and Japan 65 to 120 billion each. Early industrialisers rank far higher than their current yearly emissions suggest. Small islands have emitted almost nothing.

layers.name: Diabetes
layers.definition: Share of adults aged 20 to 79 with diabetes
layers.explanation: Pacific islands such as the Marshall Islands, Tuvalu, Nauru and Kiribati have rates above 20%, and the Gulf states are also high. Benin, Zimbabwe and Gambia are below 2%. Diet, obesity and genetics all play a part, so the map does not simply follow wealth.

layers.name: Size of the economy
layers.definition: Total yearly output of the economy in current US dollars
layers.explanation: The United States and China produce far more than anyone else, at about $26 trillion and $18 trillion. Japan, Germany, India and the United Kingdom come next at $3 to 4 trillion each. The smallest economies are Pacific islands such as Tuvalu, Nauru and Palau, each under $300 million.

layers.name: Carbon per unit of electricity
layers.definition: Grams of carbon dioxide released per kilowatt-hour of electricity
layers.unit: Grams of carbon dioxide for every kilowatt-hour.

source.name: Our World in Data (Energy Institute, Ember)

layers.explanation: Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan, which burn gas inefficiently, and small islands running on diesel release around 1,000 grams per kilowatt-hour. Hydro and nuclear countries such as Nepal, Ethiopia, Costa Rica, Bhutan, Norway and France are below 60. The map is a mirror of how much coal, oil and gas go into the grid.

layers.name: Electricity imports
layers.definition: Net electricity imports as a share of demand; negative means a net exporter
layers.unit: A percentage of electricity demand. Negative numbers are exports.

source.name: Our World in Data (Energy Institute, Ember)

layers.explanation: Laos and Paraguay export more electricity than they use at home, thanks to large dams. Luxembourg, Lithuania, Macao and Palestine import most of theirs from neighbours. Most countries sit near zero, either because they are islands or because they balance their own grid.

layers.name: Electricity use per person
layers.definition: Electricity generated per person a year

source.name: Our World in Data (Energy Institute, Ember)

layers.explanation: Iceland generates more than 50,000 kilowatt-hours per person, mostly for aluminium smelters, and Norway, Bahrain, Qatar, Kuwait and Canada are above 17,000. Chad, Somalia, Afghanistan and Sierra Leone are below 25. Rich, cold or air-conditioned countries sit at the top, and much of Africa at the bottom.

layers.name: Energy use per person
layers.definition: Primary energy used per person a year

source.name: Our World in Data (Energy Institute, Ember)

layers.explanation: Qatar, Iceland, Bahrain and Singapore each use more than 150,000 kilowatt-hours per person a year, from gas-rich industry, aluminium smelting on cheap power, or refining. Somalia, Burundi and the Central African Republic use under 300. Cold climates, heavy industry and wealth all push a country up.

layers.name: Deaths from heart disease
layers.definition: Yearly deaths from heart and circulatory disease per 100,000 people
layers.unit: A count of deaths a year for every 100,000 people.
layers.explanation: Uzbekistan, Afghanistan, Papua New Guinea and Azerbaijan lose more than 550 people per 100,000 each year to heart and circulatory disease. Japan, Peru, South Korea and France are below 90. Diet, smoking, treatment of blood pressure and the age of the population all shape the pattern, so Eastern Europe and Central Asia stand out as high.

layers.name: Human development
layers.definition: Index combining life expectancy, schooling and income, from 0 to 1
layers.explanation: Norway, Switzerland, Ireland and Iceland top the index at about 0.95, combining long lives, long schooling and high incomes. Niger, the Central African Republic and Chad sit near 0.40. Because the index blends health, schooling and income, it looks like a map of wealth but is smoother.

layers.name: Hydro electricity
layers.definition: Share of electricity from hydropower

source.name: Our World in Data (Energy Institute, Ember)

layers.explanation: Lesotho, Bhutan, Paraguay, Nepal and Albania draw nearly all their electricity from dams. Flat, dry or small countries, including most islands and the Gulf, have none. The pattern follows mountains and big rivers more than wealth.

layers.name: Income per person
layers.definition: Output of the economy per person, adjusted for prices (international dollars)
layers.unit: Dollars a person a year, adjusted for local prices.
layers.explanation: Qatar, Luxembourg and Singapore produce more than $85,000 per person once prices are adjusted. The Central African Republic, Burundi, Liberia and the Democratic Republic of the Congo are below $1,000. Western Europe, North America, Australia and the Gulf fill the top groups, while most of sub-Saharan Africa fills the lowest.

layers.name: Inflation
layers.definition: Yearly rise in consumer prices
layers.unit: A percentage change in prices over one year.
layers.explanation: In 2022 Zimbabwe's prices rose by more than 250%, and Sudan, Lebanon, Syria, Turkey and Argentina all saw rises of 70% or more. Most of the world saw 5 to 10% as energy and food prices jumped after the pandemic. A handful of small states such as Nauru and Liechtenstein recorded falling prices.

layers.name: Land area
layers.definition: Total area of the country
layers.explanation: Russia covers about 17 million square kilometres, nearly twice as much as Canada, China or the United States. Brazil and Australia follow at above 7.5 million. The Vatican, Monaco, Nauru and Tuvalu are each under 30 square kilometres.

layers.name: Latitude
layers.definition: Latitude of the centre of the country, in degrees north; negative is south
layers.unit: Degrees of latitude. Negative numbers are south of the equator.
layers.explanation: Greenland, Iceland and the Nordic countries are centred above 60 degrees north. New Zealand, Argentina, Chile and South Africa are the furthest south among large countries. Because most land is in the northern hemisphere, only a quarter of countries have a negative value.

layers.name: Life expectancy
layers.definition: Years a newborn is expected to live
layers.explanation: Japan, Switzerland, Hong Kong and the small states of Monaco and San Marino reach 84 to 87 years. The Central African Republic, Chad, Lesotho, Nigeria and Sierra Leone are in the low 50s. Wealth, health care and the burden of infectious disease explain most of the gap, which is why sub-Saharan Africa stands out.

layers.name: Median age
layers.definition: Age that splits the population into an older and a younger half
layers.explanation: Japan, Italy and Germany have median ages above 46 after decades of small families and long lives. Niger, Mali, Uganda and Chad are below 17, because large families keep most of the population young. Europe and East Asia are old, Africa is young, and the Americas and the rest of Asia fall between.

layers.name: Methane per person
layers.definition: Methane emissions per person a year, in carbon dioxide equivalents
layers.unit: Tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent a person a year.

source.name: Our World in Data (Global Carbon Project)

layers.explanation: Bahrain, Mongolia, Kuwait and Qatar top the map through gas production, and Uruguay and New Zealand through their large herds of cattle and sheep. Japan and small, densely built places such as Macao are at the bottom. Livestock, gas fields and landfill decide the pattern.

layers.name: Neighbouring countries
layers.definition: Number of countries sharing a land border
layers.explanation: China and Russia each border 14 or more countries, and Brazil 10. Germany, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Zambia are also high. Islands have none, so the Pacific, the Caribbean and Japan sit at the bottom.

layers.name: Nuclear electricity
layers.definition: Share of electricity from nuclear power

source.name: Our World in Data (Energy Institute, Ember)

layers.explanation: France gets more than 60% of its electricity from nuclear plants, and Slovakia, Ukraine, Belgium and Hungary more than 40%. Only about 30 countries have any nuclear power, so most of the map shows zero. The top groups are concentrated in Europe, North America and East Asia.

layers.name: Official languages
layers.definition: Number of official languages
layers.explanation: Zimbabwe recognises more than a dozen official languages, South Africa 11 and Namibia 9. Switzerland, Singapore and Bolivia also have several. Most countries have just one, so the high groups are small.

layers.name: People aged 65 and over
layers.definition: Share of the population aged 65 years or older
layers.explanation: More than a quarter of Japan's people are 65 or older, and Italy, Portugal, Germany and Finland are above a fifth. The Gulf states are lowest of all, below 2.5%, because most residents are working-age migrants. Sub-Saharan Africa is also low, with large young generations and shorter lives.

layers.name: Population
layers.definition: Number of people living in the country
layers.explanation: China and India each have more than 1.4 billion people, and together they hold about a third of humanity. The United States, Indonesia, Pakistan and Nigeria follow, each above 200 million. The smallest populations are tiny islands and city states such as Pitcairn, the Vatican and Niue.

layers.name: Population density
layers.definition: People per square kilometre of land
layers.unit: A count of people for every square kilometre.
layers.explanation: Monaco, Singapore and Hong Kong pack several thousand people into each square kilometre. Bangladesh is the most crowded large country, while Greenland, Mongolia, Namibia and Australia have fewer than four people per square kilometre. Western Europe and South and East Asia sit in the upper groups, and big dry or cold countries sit at the bottom.

layers.name: Renewable electricity
layers.definition: Share of electricity from renewable sources

source.name: Our World in Data (Energy Institute, Ember)

layers.explanation: Paraguay, Nepal, Iceland, Ethiopia and the Democratic Republic of the Congo get essentially all their electricity from renewables, mostly rivers. Gulf states and many small islands run almost entirely on oil and gas. Hydro-rich mountain and tropical countries score high regardless of wealth.

layers.name: Solar electricity
layers.definition: Share of electricity from solar power

source.name: Our World in Data (Energy Institute, Ember)

layers.explanation: Namibia, Palestine, Lebanon and Luxembourg got more than a fifth of their electricity from the sun in 2022, often because other supplies are scarce or expensive. Chile, Australia, Spain and Greece are also high among larger economies. Many countries still had no solar at all.

layers.name: Wind electricity
layers.definition: Share of electricity from wind power

source.name: Our World in Data (Energy Institute, Ember)

layers.explanation: Denmark gets more than half of its electricity from wind, and Lithuania, Ireland, Uruguay and Portugal more than a quarter. Windy coasts facing the Atlantic and the North Sea dominate the top group. Most of Africa, the Middle East and the Pacific have little or none.
